=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer review of Seller's SPA positions and Disclosure Letter

**Bottom line:** The Seller's package shifts most of the known risk onto the Buyer. It caps and time-limits all warranty claims tightly, treats fundamental and tax warranties as ordinary warranties, lets the Seller disclose the entire data room, and bars claims for anything the Buyer knew or could have found there. Several known issues are left to "post-Completion" resolution or are characterised as ordinary course. The package should not be accepted as a basis for mark-up. It needs a restructured approach to known matters.

**On the "FINAL" label and market claims:** The cover note says these positions were settled at principal level and are not to be re-opened. I can't verify that from the material provided, and the Seller's market-range assertions are their characterisation, not authority. Ask for the principal-level term sheet or correspondence recording the agreed positions. Have the deal team benchmark the market points against precedent or advisers' data before accepting them as an anchor.

---

## 1. Liability cap (cl 12.1): AUD 4.8m (20% of price)

**Departure:** A 20% cap on general warranties, with no separate higher cap for fundamental or tax warranties (see section 4), and with known matters likely to fall inside it.

**Reasoning:** The known exposures are substantial: Riverlark debt of about AUD 3.2m, employee bonuses of AUD 420k before on-costs, Ironquay AUD 180k, and supplier renewals of AUD 330k. Together that is about AUD 4.1m before counting Bluefen (about 30% of FY26 revenue) or the privacy incident. If any of these come through warranty claims, they consume most of the cap. Known matters should be dealt with through price, conditions or specific indemnities that sit outside the cap, not through the general warranty regime.

**Push back:** Raise the general cap materially (open high, with a fallback the deal team sets), and carve specific indemnities, fundamental warranties, tax and fraud out of the cap altogether.

## 2. Thresholds (cl 12.2): AUD 25k de minimis and AUD 250k true-deductible basket

**Departure:** The basket is about 1.04% of price and operates as a deductible, so only the amount above AUD 250k is recoverable. The de minimis of AUD 25k excludes individual claims below that level, so a series of smaller related issues (for example, several supplier or privacy-related items) can fall entirely outside recovery.

**Push back:**
- Replace the deductible with a **tipping (first-dollar) basket**, with a lower threshold (the deal team should set the figure, below the Seller's 1%).
- Reduce the de minimis, and aggregate related claims arising from the same facts.
- Confirm that the thresholds do not apply to specific indemnities, fundamental warranties or tax.

## 3. Time limits (cl 12.3 / 13): 18 months, applying to all claims

**Departure:** The 18-month period is short for a SaaS business with a privacy incident under review, an IP dispute over Ironquay materials, and unresolved tax positions. The Seller's proposal that the limitation "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" would bring fundamental and tax claims into the 18-month window by default.

**Reasoning:** The Limitation Act 1969 (NSW) sets a default 6-year period for contract claims, and a contract can shorten it. Under the Seller's drafting, the Buyer would lose that protection for claims that take time to surface, such as tax assessments or privacy regulator action. Check the precise effect with NSW counsel.

**Push back:**
- General warranties: 36 months (fallback 24).
- Tax: ATO/State assessment period plus a buffer.
- Fundamental (title, capacity) and fraud: 6 years, or the full statutory period.
- Delete the "applies to all Claims" default. Each category should have its own period.

## 4. Fundamental and title warranties (cl 12 generally)

**Departure:** The Seller would subject capacity and title to the same cap and time limits as general warranties "for administrative simplicity."

**Reasoning:** Title and capacity go to whether the Buyer gets what it is paying for. Capping them at 20% of the price means the Buyer could pay AUD 24m for shares it doesn't fully own, with recovery limited to AUD 4.8m. Title is also only evidenced by the Seller's own share register at DD-012, with no independent verification.

**Push back:**
- Title and capacity capped at the full purchase price, with the longer time limit above.
- Require an ASIC current company extract, a certified share register, evidence of no encumbrances over the shares, and a title warranty with indemnity.
- Do not accept DD-012 as sufficient verification. The Disclosure Letter itself (para 10) says the Buyer has not completed its own verification.

## 5. Exclusive remedy, limitations and non-reliance (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Departure:** The limitation, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to "all Claims of any nature."

**Push back:** Carve out fraud (non-reliance and exclusive-remedy clauses generally cannot exclude liability for fraud, but the drafting should say so expressly), specific indemnities, title, tax, and claims under the completion mechanics. Exclusive remedy should not stop the Buyer from pursuing price adjustment or specific performance of conditions. Confirm with NSW counsel how these clauses operate with the Australian Consumer Law and general contract principles, though the ACL should not apply to a B2B share sale.

## 6. Buyer knowledge and data room disclosure (cl 8.3; Disclosure Letter paras 1.1, 1.2; Schedule 7)

**Departure:** This is the most serious structural issue. The Seller:
- discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room (through 22 Sept 2026), plus the Accounts, statutory registers and public records;
- bars the Buyer from claiming for anything it or its advisers knew, including anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records.

**Reasoning:** Together these would qualify the warranties against the whole data room and remove the Buyer's ability to claim for anything in it. This is a broad, unspecific disclosure that effectively neutralises the warranties. The Buyer's knowledge of the known issues would be used against it. Australian law on whether a buyer's knowledge bars a warranty claim is not settled in a way that protects the Buyer, so the contract needs to say so.

**Push back:**
- Delete cl 8.3 and the general disclosure in paras 1.1 and 1.2.
- Disclosure only against specific, fairly disclosed matters, not a general reference to documents.
- Add an express clause that the Buyer's knowledge (actual or constructive, and through its advisers) does not prejudice any claim (a "pro-sandbagging" clause).
- Known issues should be handled through price, conditions or specific indemnities, not warranty disclosure.

## 7. Bluefen change-control consent (cl 3 / 6.3; Disclosure Letter para 2)

**Departure:** The Seller will use "reasonable endeavours" and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. The Disclosure Letter confirms no final written consent exists and that the conditions in cl 11.3 are unsatisfied.

**Reasoning:** Bluefen is about 30% of FY26 revenue. Reasonable endeavours is a weak obligation, and "delivery of written consent" does not require the consent to be unconditional, on acceptable terms, or free of changes to the commercial relationship. The clause also doesn't say what happens if consent is refused.

**Push back:**
- Make Bluefen consent, in agreed form and without adverse variation, a **condition precedent**, with a Buyer walk-right if not satisfied by a long-stop date.
- Require satisfaction of cl 11.3 conditions as a deliverable.
- If the Buyer waives, add a specific indemnity or price adjustment for revenue loss if Bluefen terminates or varies within a set period after Completion.

## 8. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7; Disclosure Letter para 3)

**Departure:** About AUD 3.2m outstanding, with the release to be provided "following Completion." The Disclosure Letter says the facility has not been repaid and no discharge is included.

**Reasoning:** This is a debt-free, cash-free deal. The Buyer should not take on secured debt and rely on a post-Completion release. Until the facility is repaid and security is discharged, the Buyer is exposed to the lender's enforcement rights over the company's assets. The Riverlark change-of-control clause (8.1) may also be triggered by the share sale, and the disclosure does not say whether it is.

**Push back:**
- Repayment at Completion through the funds flow, with a payoff letter and discharge of all security, including PPSR registrations and any guarantees, delivered at or before Completion.
- Confirm that the debt is deducted from the price as Indebtedness.
- Confirm whether the change-of-control clause is triggered, and obtain a waiver if so.

## 9. Ironquay IP and SOW3 (cl 11.1; Disclosure Letter para 4)

**Departure:** The indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment, which the Seller says is adequate. DD-004 cl 7.3 makes transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials conditional on payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open, with no receipt or confirmatory assignment in the data room.

**Reasoning:** The real risk is not the AUD 180k. It is that the company does not own the IP it uses. A narrow indemnity tied to one payment doesn't address ownership, and the AUD 180k itself is only indicative (it is not bank-verified).

**Push back:**
- Payment of all outstanding SOW fees before Completion, from the Seller's proceeds if necessary.
- A confirmatory assignment of Project Materials as a condition precedent.
- An IP ownership warranty and a specific indemnity covering all Ironquay claims, not just SOW3, outside the general cap.

## 10. Employee bonuses (DD-005; Disclosure Letter para 5)

**Departure:** AUD 420k of conditional Completion bonuses are described as "a matter for the Seller" and not included in the funds flow. The disclosure does not say whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

**Reasoning:** If the bonuses are payable by the company after Completion, the Buyer bears them unless the price reflects them. Payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs add to the cost, and conditions based on continued employment make the amount uncertain.

**Push back:**
- All Completion bonuses, with employer on-costs, payroll tax and super, treated as Seller-borne Transaction Expenses or debt-like items deducted from price, and paid through the funds flow.
- A bonus schedule and payroll tax calculation before signing.
- A Seller indemnity for any residual bonus or employment-related liability.

## 11. Privacy and export incident (cl 4.6 / Schedule 6; DD-006; Disclosure Letter para 6)

**Departure:** The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." The export may contain about 1,240 records with names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. The disclosure does not establish whether anyone unauthorised accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. No loss amount is stated.

**Reasoning:** This is a potential data breach with an open investigation. Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must carry out an assessment promptly, and generally within 30 days, and notify if required. Depending on when the company became aware, that window may have passed or be about to pass. The Seller's characterisation cannot be relied on while the investigation is open. Privacy regulator action, notification costs and customer claims could all arise after Completion.

**Push back:**
- Require a forensic investigation report and the company's NDB assessment as a pre-signing or pre-Completion deliverable, including the date the company became aware.
- A specific, uncapped (or separately capped) indemnity for privacy and data breach losses, including regulatory penalties, notification costs and third-party claims, outside the basket and de minimis.
- A specific warranty that no eligible data breach has occurred to the Seller's knowledge, except as fully disclosed.
- A Seller obligation to cooperate in any regulator inquiry.

## 12. Office lease (Disclosure Letter para 7)

**Departure:** The notification obligation is identified, but the Seller does not say whether landlord consent to the share sale is needed.

**Push back:** Obtain a legal review of the lease. If consent is required, make it a condition precedent. If not, obtain written confirmation from the landlord or a Seller warranty.

## 13. Supplier renewals (DD-008, DD-011; Disclosure Letter para 8)

**Departure:** The Seller calls the three renewals (AUD 330k aggregate) ordinary-course costs. The disclosure does not say whether each is unavoidable, terminable, or accrued. The renewals are described as related and read together for timing and scope.

**Reasoning:** Ordinary-course characterisation is the Seller's view. If the renewals are multi-year commitments entered into before Completion, the Buyer may inherit obligations beyond the pre-Completion period. Overlap between the documents may also mean the aggregate figure is overstated or understated.

**Push back:** Obtain the underlying contracts. Require the Seller to bear any renewal cost attributable to the pre-Completion period, or treat unpaid renewal commitments as debt-like items. Require a warranty that no renewal is outside the ordinary course.

## 14. Mossvale assignment restriction (Disclosure Letter para 9)

**Departure:** The provision restricts assignment, but the Seller does not say whether a share sale triggers the restriction.

**Push back:** Obtain a legal opinion or the counterparty's written confirmation. If consent is needed, make it a condition precedent.

## 15. Tax and IP warranties ("settled under the general regime")

**Departure:** The Seller treats tax and IP as covered by the general regime (cap and time limits above).

**Push back:** Tax is a classic specific indemnity area. Require a pre-Completion tax indemnity uncapped to price, a longer time limit (see section 3), and a separate tax warranty set. IP should sit under the ownership warranty in section 9.

## 16. Disclosure timing and bring-down

**Departure:** The data room and disclosure are as at 22 September 2026. Today is 5 November 2026.

**Push back:** Require a bring-down disclosure at signing and Completion, with warranties repeated at Completion. Confirm the Buyer's right to walk away or claim if matters change between signing and Completion.

---

## Summary of recommendations

**Structural (highest priority)**
1. Reject the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing. Ask for the principal-level record.
2. Delete the buyer-knowledge bar (cl 8.3) and general data room and register disclosure (paras 1.1, 1.2). Add pro-sandbagging language.
3. Address known matters through conditions, price adjustments and specific indemnities outside the general cap, not through warranties.

**Liability and time limits**
4. Raise the general cap well above 20%. Carve out specific indemnities, fundamental warranties, tax and fraud, capped at price or uncapped as the deal team decides.
5. Replace the deductible basket with a tipping basket at a lower level, reduce the de minimis, and aggregate related claims.
6. Set general warranty time limits at 36 months (fallback 24), tax at the assessment period plus a buffer, and fundamental warranties and fraud at 6 years. Remove the "applies to all Claims" default.

**Fundamental and title**
7. Cap title and capacity at the full price, with the longer time limit. Require ASIC extract, certified share register, and evidence of no encumbrances over the shares.

**Known matters**
8. Bluefen: make written consent in agreed form a condition precedent with a walk-right, and add a revenue-loss indemnity if waived.
9. Riverlark: repay and discharge all security at Completion through the funds flow; deduct as Indebtedness.
10. Ironquay: payment of all SOW fees and a confirmatory IP assignment before Completion, plus an IP ownership indemnity covering all Ironquay claims.
11. Bonuses: include the AUD 420k with on-costs, payroll tax and super as Seller-borne Transaction Expenses in the funds flow; obtain a bonus schedule.
12. Privacy incident: forensic report and NDB assessment before Completion (confirm the awareness date now), plus an uncapped, specific privacy indemnity.
13. Lease, Mossvale and any change-of-control triggers: obtain legal confirmation; make consents conditions precedent where required.
14. Supplier renewals: obtain contracts; allocate pre-Completion cost to the Seller.

**Process**
15. Bring-down disclosure at signing and Completion, with warranties repeated at Completion.
16. Have NSW counsel confirm the statutory limitation position, the enforceability of non-reliance and knowledge clauses, and NDB obligations under the Privacy Act. These are points I have flagged for verification rather than settled conclusions.

The known matters above total well over AUD 4m in quantifiable items before Bluefen revenue and the privacy exposure are considered. The figures are indicative from the disclosure, not a valuation, and the deal team should confirm them against the underlying documents.

**Departure:** The indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment, which the Seller says is adequate. DD-004 cl 7.3 makes transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials conditional on payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open, with no receipt or confirmatory assignment in the data room.

**Reasoning:** The real risk is not the AUD 180k. It is that the company does not own the IP it uses. A narrow indemnity tied to one payment doesn't address ownership, and the AUD 180k itself is only indicative (it is not bank-verified).

**Push back:**
- Payment of all outstanding SOW fees before Completion, from the Seller's proceeds if necessary.
- A confirmatory assignment of Project Materials as a condition precedent.
- An IP ownership warranty and a specific indemnity covering all Ironquay claims, not just SOW3, outside the general cap.

## 10. Employee bonuses (DD-005; Disclosure Letter para 5)

**Departure:** AUD 420k of conditional Completion bonuses are described as "a matter for the Seller" and not included in the funds flow. The disclosure does not say whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

**Reasoning:** If the bonuses are payable by the company after Completion, the Buyer bears them unless the price reflects them. Payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs add to the cost, and conditions based on continued employment make the amount uncertain.

**Push back:**
- All Completion bonuses, with employer on-costs, payroll tax and super, treated as Seller-borne Transaction Expenses or debt-like items deducted from price, and paid through the funds flow.
- A bonus schedule and payroll tax calculation before signing.
- A Seller indemnity for any residual bonus or employment-related liability.

## 11. Privacy and export incident (cl 4.6 / Schedule 6; DD-006; Disclosure Letter para 6)

**Departure:** The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." The export may contain about 1,240 records with names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. The disclosure does not establish whether anyone unauthorised accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. No loss amount is stated.

**Reasoning:** This is a potential data breach with an open investigation. Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must carry out an assessment promptly, and generally within 30 days, and notify if required. Depending on when the company became aware, that window may have passed or be about to pass. The Seller's characterisation cannot be relied on while the investigation is open. Privacy regulator action, notification costs and customer claims could all arise after Completion.

**Push back:**
- Require a forensic investigation report and the company's NDB assessment as a pre-signing or pre-Completion deliverable, including the date the company became aware.
- A specific, uncapped (or separately capped) indemnity for privacy and data breach losses, including regulatory penalties, notification costs and third-party claims, outside the basket and de minimis.
- A specific warranty that no eligible data breach has occurred to the Seller's knowledge, except as fully disclosed.
- A Seller obligation to cooperate in any regulator inquiry.

## 12. Office lease (Disclosure Letter para 7)

**Departure:** The notification obligation is identified, but the Seller does not say whether landlord consent to the share sale is needed.

**Push back:** Obtain a legal review of the lease. If consent is required, make it a condition precedent. If not, obtain written confirmation from the landlord or a Seller warranty.

## 13. Supplier renewals (DD-008, DD-011; Disclosure Letter para 8)

**Departure:** The Seller calls the three renewals (AUD 330k aggregate) ordinary-course costs. The disclosure does not say whether each is unavoidable, terminable, or accrued. The renewals are described as related and read together for timing and scope.

**Reasoning:** Ordinary-course characterisation is the Seller's view. If the renewals are multi-year commitments entered into before Completion, the Buyer may inherit obligations beyond the pre-Completion period. Overlap between the documents may also mean the aggregate figure is overstated or understated.

**Push back:** Obtain the underlying contracts. Require the Seller to bear any renewal cost attributable to the pre-Completion period, or treat unpaid renewal commitments as debt-like items. Require a warranty that no renewal is outside the ordinary course.

## 14. Mossvale assignment restriction (Disclosure Letter para 9)

**Departure:** The provision restricts assignment, but the Seller does not say whether a share sale triggers the restriction.

**Push back:** Obtain a legal opinion or the counterparty's written confirmation. If consent is needed, make it a condition precedent.

## 15. Tax and IP warranties ("settled under the general regime")

**Departure:** The Seller treats tax and IP as covered by the general regime (cap and time limits above).

**Push back:** Tax is a classic specific indemnity area. Require a pre-Completion tax indemnity uncapped to price, a longer time limit (see section 3), and a separate tax warranty set. IP should sit under the ownership warranty in section 9.

## 16. Disclosure timing and bring-down

**Departure:** The data room and disclosure are as at 22 September 2026. Today is 5 November 2026.

**Push back:** Require a bring-down disclosure at signing and Completion, with warranties repeated at Completion. Confirm the Buyer's right to walk away or claim if matters change between signing and Completion.

## Summary of recommendations

**Structural (highest priority)**
1. Reject the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing. Ask for the principal-level record.
2. Delete the buyer-knowledge bar (cl 8.3) and general data room and register disclosure (paras 1.1, 1.2). Add pro-sandbagging language.
3. Address known matters through conditions, price adjustments and specific indemnities outside the general cap, not through warranties.

**Liability and time limits**
4. Raise the general cap well above 20%. Carve out specific indemnities, fundamental warranties, tax and fraud, capped at price or uncapped as the deal team decides.
5. Replace the deductible basket with a tipping basket at a lower level, reduce the de minimis, and aggregate related claims.
6. Set general warranty time limits at 36 months (fallback 24), tax at the assessment period plus a buffer, and fundamental warranties and fraud at 6 years. Remove the "applies to all Claims" default.

**Fundamental and title**
7. Cap title and capacity at the full price, with the longer time limit. Require ASIC extract, certified share register, and evidence of no encumbrances over the shares.

**Known matters**
8. Bluefen: make written consent in agreed form a condition precedent with a walk-right, and add a revenue-loss indemnity if waived.
9. Riverlark: repay and discharge all security at Completion through the funds flow; deduct as Indebtedness.
10. Ironquay: payment of all SOW fees and a confirmatory IP assignment before Completion, plus an IP ownership indemnity covering all Ironquay claims.
11. Bonuses: include the AUD 420k with on-costs, payroll tax and super as Seller-borne Transaction Expenses in the funds flow; obtain a bonus schedule.
12. Privacy incident: forensic report and NDB assessment before Completion (confirm the awareness date now), plus an uncapped, specific privacy indemnity.
13. Lease, Mossvale and any change-of-control triggers: obtain legal confirmation; make consents conditions precedent where required.
14. Supplier renewals: obtain contracts; allocate pre-Completion cost to the Seller.

**Process**
15. Bring-down disclosure at signing and Completion, with warranties repeated at Completion.
16. Have NSW counsel confirm the statutory limitation position, the enforceability of non-reliance and knowledge clauses, and NDB obligations under the Privacy Act. These are points I have flagged for verification rather than settled conclusions.

The known matters above total well over AUD 4m in quantifiable items before Bluefen revenue and the privacy exposure are considered. The figures are indicative from the disclosure, not a valuation, and the deal team should confirm them against the underlying documents.
